1.pericope_label: The kings' hearts melted; circumcise again the children of Israel

schools.summary: Read the terror by asking who broke last. The people's hearts had fainted already -- Rahab said so to the spies -- but the kings had kept their spirits up, promising themselves that with a populous country and fortified cities they could hold against invaders. What broke them was not that Israel crossed but that Israel crossed by a miracle, with the God of nature manifestly fighting for them. Then make the timing of the command do the theological work. God ordered the circumcision at exactly the moment the land was in consternation, because only then could it be done safely in an enemy's country: their hearts being melted, their hands were tied, and they could not take the advantage Simeon and Levi took against the Shechemites while those men were sore. Press what follows from that. Joshua could not be sure the paralysis would hold, so had he ordered a general circumcision on his own judgment he might justly have been censured as imprudent -- the thing good in itself, but in the eye of reason unseasonable. Because God commanded it, he must not consult with flesh and blood; and he that bade them do it would bear them out in it.

Attend to what the fear did not do. It left the Canaanites destitute of counsel and strength, but it did not incline their minds to seek a remedy; unbelievers when smitten with fear cease not to wrestle with God, so the dread that ought to have urged them to caution only hurried them on headlong. And say plainly whose benefit it was for: they were terrified from above for the sake of the people, so that the enemy was already routed before the conflict began. Then turn on the long neglect that made the circumcision necessary, and refuse the excuse commonly offered. That a people constantly under arms had no leisure is a frivolous apology; nothing ought to have weighed so much with them as the word spoken to Abraham, and even had there been real danger to the infants the right course was to trust the paternal providence of God. The omission could have originated in nothing but distrust, for the seal of the covenant was more precious than a hundred lives. Fix the occasion exactly as the text does: it was when the dread had seized the inhabitants that the moment became fit for what was next ordered.

Ask why a people with iron would circumcise with stone, and answer it with evidence rather than assertion. Metal was probably unlawful in the rite: Zipporah took a sharp stone; the Egyptians held it profane to use metal for incisions in preparing a body; the altar had to be of unhewn stones lest a tool of iron pollute it; and an Ethiopian tribe following the Mosaic institution still circumcises with knives of stone. Add the physical reason if it helps, that a stone edge leaves no metal particles to oxidize in the wound, so it inflames less and heals sooner. On the local situation, explain why the Canaanites had grown careless -- Jordan was their bulwark, the Israelites had lingered in the neighbouring country without attacking, and the river was in flood -- and see providence in their paralysis, that Israel might quietly receive circumcision and the passover before any fighting began. On the second time, refuse to press the phrase: it is a second circumcision with respect to the body of the people, part having been circumcised before, not the same persons circumcised twice.

Settle the words before settling the picture. The expression rendered sharp knives is knives of tsurim, and the word does not elsewhere denote the material of a tool but its edge, so keen-edged knives is the better translation -- though they may have been stone all the same, and an addition in the Greek at the end of the book has the stone knives buried with Joshua. Compare the other places where the word plainly means edge. On the second time, do not press the ordinal: it is added to give emphasis, and means circumcise the people again as it once was circumcised, not that the same act had once before been performed on the same men. Then state the necessity in order: all who came out of Egypt were circumcised, circumcision was neglected on the journey, so the nation was no longer a circumcised nation, and the law had to be imposed as an inviolable obligation before the passover could be kept a few days later. Identify the nations named as representative of the rest and leave it there.

debates.question: Were the knives of flint, or merely sharp?

sides.position: Of stone, because metal was probably unlawful in the rite: Zipporah used a sharp stone, the Egyptians held metal profane for incisions in a body, the altar had to be unhewn, and an Ethiopian tribe still circumcises with stone; a stone edge also leaves no metal particles to inflame the wound

Merely keen-edged, since the Hebrew word denotes the edge of a tool and not its material; though they may have been stone all the same, as an addition in the Greek at the end of the book buries the stone knives with Joshua

debates.question: Why was the command given at this precise moment?

sides.position: Because the enemy's terror made it safe: their hearts being melted their hands were tied, so they could not do as Simeon and Levi did to the Shechemites; Joshua could not have known that, which is why it had to be commanded rather than devised
Because the dread that had seized the inhabitants made it a fit time for what was next ordered
The question of timing matters less than the long neglect: the usual excuse that a people under arms had no leisure is frivolous, and the omission could have originated only in distrust

outliers.note: Alone refuses to excuse the forty years' neglect, calling the standard apology frivolous, holding that even a real danger to the infants should have been met by trusting the paternal providence of God, and concluding that the omission could have originated in nothing but distrust, since the seal of the covenant was more precious than a hundred lives.

Alone disputes the rendering of the knives on lexical grounds, holding that the Hebrew word denotes the edge of a tool rather than its material, so that keen-edged is the better translation, while granting that they may have been stone all the same.

themes: their heart melted, neither was there spirit in them any more, because of the children of Israel
Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again the children of Israel the second time
all the kings of the Amorites... and all the kings of the Canaanites, which were by the sea

3.pericope_label: The hill of the foreskins; the generation raised up in their stead

schools.summary: Name the place from what happened there -- the spot was afterwards called the hill of the foreskins because the foreskins were buried in it -- and state the reason for the rite in the order the text gives: every man who came out of Egypt was circumcised, all who died in the wilderness died under sentence for not hearkening to the voice of the Lord, and their sons, raised up in their place, were the uncircumcised generation Joshua circumcised. Then take up the phrase reproach of Egypt, which does not explain itself, since everyone born in Egypt had been circumcised. Notice that the years of wandering are a blank in the narrative: the chapters of Numbers belonging to that period record no progress in time or place. A people who had turned back in their hearts to Egypt bore the reproach of that apostasy, and under the breach of promise they omitted the sign of the covenant as though they were no longer the people of God. On that reading the passage of Jordan is the practical proof of their restoration. Note also that the first person used here suggests the whole passage is framed as the fathers' answer to the children's question.

Explain how so large a work was done so fast, and why it had to be. Joshua caused the circumcision rather than performing it, and because the passover was approaching it had to be quick, so many hands were used; it is likely enough that the Israelites settled beyond Jordan were circumcised at the same time. On why it had lapsed, give the lenient answer first and then decline it: the parents or the rulers may have omitted it by divine permission, since the passover itself might be neglected on a journey, but it is better read as a continued token of God's displeasure for their unbelief and murmuring, a standing sign that they should never have the benefit of the promise circumcision sealed. Then list what the rite accomplished now: a testimony that God was reconciled and would not further impute the parents' rebellion, the removal of the impediment of constant travel, preparation for the feast, distinction from the Canaanites whose land they had entered, and ratification of the covenant that gave them the land. And note the sharpness of the wording, that the term used of them commonly means the Gentiles, marking them unworthy the name of Israelites, and that the sentence denied them so much as a sight of the land, which was granted to Moses. Add that God dispensed with the rite for a time because of their unsettled state, but that another passover made it necessary again, since no uncircumcised man could be reckoned within the covenant or eat the feast that sealed it; and draw the parallel your own church follows, that as baptism succeeded circumcision and the Supper succeeded the passover, none is admitted to the one before receiving the other.

Remove the difficulty the English creates before drawing any lesson. Joshua no more circumcised the people with his own hand than he made the knives with his own hand; he ordered both and saw them done. And the rite was never restricted to any order of men, not to priests or Levites, so anyone might perform it -- which is why a work that looks impossibly large could be finished quickly. On when the earlier general circumcision took place, weigh the options and say which is likeliest: during the three days' darkness in Egypt, when the Egyptians could take no advantage of it as Simeon and Levi did of the Shechemites, is more probable than the night of the departure, when many would have been unfit to travel, and preferable to Sinai a year later. Keep the arithmetic honest as well: the forty years is a round number, short by a few days, and not the forty-two of the Greek version.

debates.question: Why was circumcision omitted for a generation?

sides.position: By dispensation, God setting the obligation aside for a time because of their unsettled state

By permission at first, since the passover itself might be neglected on a journey; but better read as a continued token of God's displeasure, a sign that they should never have the benefit of the promise circumcision sealed

Because a people who had turned back in their hearts to Egypt bore the reproach of that apostasy and dropped the sign of the covenant as though no longer God's; the wandering years are a blank in the narrative, recording no progress in time or place

outliers.note: Alone treats the wandering years as a narrative blank, observing that the chapters of Numbers belonging to that period record no note of progress in time or place, and reading the dropped sign of the covenant as the mark of a people who had turned back in their hearts to Egypt.

Alone removes the difficulty that Joshua could not personally have circumcised a nation, pointing out that the rite was never restricted to priests or Levites, so that anyone might perform it and the work could be finished quickly.

themes: Joshua made him sharp knives, and circumcised the children of Israel at the hill of the foreskins
all the people that were born in the wilderness by the way as they came forth out of Egypt, them they had not circumcised
their children, whom he raised up in their stead, them Joshua circumcised

8.pericope_label: They abode in the camp till whole; the reproach of Egypt rolled away

schools.summary: Measure the risk honestly before praising the obedience. Travellers report that adults who are circumcised keep their beds about three weeks and can walk only with great difficulty, so ask the obvious question: how were they not attacked and destroyed, as the Shechemites were in exactly this condition? Joshua as an able general would have seen at once that the measure exposed his whole host to annihilation, and in the teeth of his enemies he reduced the greater part of his army to total helplessness, trusting the arm of God alone; and God did not permit one enemy to disturb them. Then ask the harder question, why the order did not come while they were still safe east of Jordan, and answer it: God chose to bring them into straits where no counsel or might but his own could save them, so that the excellence of the power might plainly be his. Say in a sentence what that cost them -- it was an act of great faith to accept such pain and danger hemmed in between the river and their enemies. On the reproach itself, take it as uncircumcision, which made them resemble the uncircumcised Egyptians, and note that this proves Israel did not receive the rite from Egypt, since they would not have held abominable the nation that gave them the mark of purity.

Test the received readings of the reproach of Egypt one by one, and say which you reject and why. That they would no longer be scorned by the Egyptians as though God had deceived them is too far fetched; that they would no longer lie under the imputation of worshipping Egypt's gods is not the sense either. Take it rather that they were freed from an invidious charge that otherwise overbore them. It was disreputable to have thrown off the yoke and revolted from the king under whom they lived, and since they gave out that God was the avenger of unjust tyranny they could easily be upbraided with using his name as a colour for desertion. The renewal of the ancient covenant, sealed in their flesh before ever they went down to Egypt, wiped the charge away: their liberty was restored by God, who had long since taken them under his protection. Name the place from that removal of disgrace, and set aside the fancy that the cut foreskin was called Gilgal because it made a kind of circle -- that abandons the literal meaning for an unnecessary fiction. Note also that the work seems to have been finished in a single day.

Read the genitive the other way and see what follows. The reproach of Egypt is the reproach proceeding from Egypt, as the reproach of Moab elsewhere is the reproach heaped upon Israel by Moab. It is therefore not the Egyptian bondage, nor the misery still clinging to them from Egypt, but the taunt in Egyptian mouths that Jehovah brought this people out only to destroy them in the desert -- a reproach that stood against Israel exactly as long as it was condemned to wander and die there, and that the circumcision rolled away. Then, rather than settling the phrase further, set beside it what it anticipates: the promise that the Lord will swallow up death in victory and take the rebuke of his people from off all the earth, the circumcision made without hands in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, and the hour when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption.

debates.question: What is the reproach of Egypt?

sides.position: Uncircumcision itself, which made Israel resemble the uncircumcised Egyptians, whom the Hebrews held to be grossly impure; which also proves Israel did not take the rite from Egypt

Uncircumcision, called Egyptian either because the neighbouring nations descended from Abraham by the concubines were circumcised and the Egyptians were not, or because Israel coming out of Egypt was reckoned a sort of Egyptian, or because many had neglected the duty there for worldly reasons
The reproach proceeding from Egypt, that is the Egyptian taunt that Jehovah brought the people out only to destroy them in the desert, which stood as long as Israel wandered and died there
Neither of the usual readings but a political charge: that they were deserters and rebels against legitimate authority, an imputation the renewal of the ancient covenant wiped away

outliers.note: Alone quantifies the danger, citing a traveller's report that adults circumcised keep their beds about three weeks, and alone asks why the order did not come while Israel was still safe east of Jordan, answering that God chose to bring them into straits where no counsel or might but his own could save them.

Alone declines to argue the disputed phrase and reaches instead for what it anticipates, setting beside it the swallowing up of death in victory, the circumcision made without hands, and the putting on of incorruption.

themes: when they had done circumcising all the people... they abode in their places in the camp, till they were whole
This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you
the name of the place is called Gilgal unto this day

10.pericope_label: The passover in the plains of Jericho; the manna ceased

schools.summary: Set the passover against the soldier's usual excuse. Men taking the field think themselves excused from religious exercises, having neither time nor thought for them; Joshua opened his campaign with one act of devotion after another, and that is likely to end well which begins with God. Mark where it was kept -- in the plains of Jericho, as it were in defiance of the Canaanites round about -- and mark the sequence, circumcision and then immediately the passover, as those who received the word were baptized and immediately found breaking bread. Then say why the feast returns here. While they wandered they were denied the benefit and comfort of this ordinance as a further token of God's displeasure; now God comforts them again after the time that he afflicted them. And press the fitness of remembering the deliverance from Egypt at the very moment of entering Canaan: the finishing of mercies should bring to mind the beginning of them, and when it is perfect day we must not forget how welcome the morning light was when we long waited for it.

Refuse the common assumption that the passover lapsed for forty years, and give reasons. It is not probable that what God had lately commanded to be kept in all their generations was suddenly cast aside; how inconsistent that a perpetual ordinance should become obsolete within two years, and how heartless to bury the memory of so recent a favour that quickly. To the objection that no uncircumcised person might eat it, answer that they were dispensed from the law in this as in the other parts of legal worship they certainly did continue to observe. On the corn, take it for last year's grain, since the new could not be eaten before the wave sheaf was offered, and face the practical difficulty the reading raises -- how they reached stored grain while Jericho was shut up so that none went in or out -- offering the outlying villages, purchase from corn traders, or barns beyond the walls. Do not overstate the novelty either: they had passed through country that was not uncultivated, they ate what remained of the sacrifices, and the manna was needed only until a fuller supply came in. And read the cessation as a type: the manna standing for Christ held forth in the ordinances, which continue until all the spiritual Israel has passed over Jordan, and then cease.

Get the calendar right and let the difficulty stand where it is real. The passover was killed between the evenings of the fourteenth and eaten that night, which by Jewish reckoning belonged to the fifteenth, so the morrow after the passover is the sixteenth, when the first sheaf was offered and the rest might then be eaten; the manna failed on the seventeenth. Raise the objection to the whole scheme honestly: if the circumcision was on the eleventh and the sore at its worst on the thirteenth, a people fit to keep the feast on the fourteenth were healed miraculously rather than naturally, and one scholar has been driven to place the passover a month later on that account. On the word rendered old corn, derive it from a root meaning to pass over and read it simply as the produce, what passes from the land to the cultivator, or what passes from hand to hand in trade, that is, bought corn. On why the manna stopped, argue from providence: it continued exactly as long as it was needed and ceased when ordinary means sufficed, which is itself the proof that it was no natural production but a special gift, for God will not be prodigal of his favours by working miracles where common provision will serve.

Count the passovers and note what the count means: this is the third in Israel's history, the first in Egypt at the deliverance, the second at Sinai, and this one beyond Jordan -- two belonging to the going out and one to the coming in. Connect it to the circumcision by the law that no uncircumcised person shall eat it, which is why the wandering generation could not keep the feast. On the corn, deny that the word must mean last year's: it appears to be the produce of that very harvest, brought to the camp probably for sale, and is simply corn grown in the land of Canaan. Then take the dating of the manna seriously enough to compute it. Reckoning from its first appearance to its last, it fell thirty-nine years and eleven months, and never on a Sabbath; it kept Sabbath through the whole wilderness and kept Sabbath finally on the day of the week afterwards marked by the resurrection. Draw the consequence: it is the risen Christ who takes the place of the manna, and in the discourse where he calls himself the true bread from heaven he points again and again to resurrection as the end of the life he gives.

debates.question: Had the passover lapsed during the wilderness years?

sides.position: Yes, suspended from the time they left Sinai, and denied them as a further token of God's displeasure

No. What God had lately ordered kept in all their generations would not be cast aside within two years, and the objection that the uncircumcised could not eat it is met by the dispensation under which they continued the rest of legal worship

debates.question: What was the corn they ate?

sides.position: Last year's corn, since the new could not be eaten before the wave sheaf was offered, left in the barns by inhabitants who had fled to their strong cities
Simply the produce, from a root meaning to pass over: what passes from the land to the cultivator, or on another authority what passes from hand to hand in trade, that is bought corn
Not necessarily last year's at all, but the produce of that very harvest, brought to the camp probably for sale

debates.question: On what day did the manna cease?

sides.position: The seventeenth, since the sheaf was offered on the sixteenth in broad daylight while the manna fell only at night or very early

The sixteenth; and reckoned from its first appearance it fell thirty-nine years and eleven months, always resting on the Sabbath, ceasing at last on the day of the week afterwards marked by the resurrection

outliers.note: Alone denies that the passover lapsed in the wilderness, arguing that a perpetual ordinance would not become obsolete within two years and that it would have been heartless to bury the memory of so recent a favour that quickly.

Alone computes the whole span of the manna, finding that it fell thirty-nine years and eleven months and always rested on the Sabbath, and that it kept Sabbath finally on the day of the week later marked by the resurrection, so that the risen Christ takes the place of the bread from heaven.

themes: the children of Israel encamped in Gilgal, and kept the passover on the fourteenth day of the month at even
they did eat of the old corn of the land on the morrow after the passover, unleavened cakes, and parched corn
the manna ceased on the morrow after they had eaten of the old corn of the land

13.pericope_label: A man with his sword drawn; captain of the host of the LORD

schools.summary: Note when the vision came, because the timing is the lesson: immediately after the circumcision and the passover were performed. We may expect discoveries of divine grace when we are found in the way of our duty and are diligent in our attendance on holy ordinances. Note where he was -- alone, fearless of danger because sure of protection, either meditating and praying, or surveying the fortifications and at a loss how to make his approach. Either way God will help those that help themselves; the law succours those who watch, not those who sleep. Joshua was in his post as a general when God made himself known as Generalissimo. Then describe the appearance as it happened: a man full of thought and care, eyes fixed on the ground, surprised into lifting them. To Abraham in his tent he had appeared as a traveller; to Joshua in the field as a man of war, for Christ will be to his people what their faith expects and desires. Make the drawn sword do two things -- justify the war, since when the sovereign draws the sword war is proclaimed and the subject is authorized to draw too, and encourage its vigorous prosecution, since that sword turns every way for the defence of his people.

Establish that the vision was real before arguing what it meant. That he lifted up his eyes is said to guard against the suspicion that his sight was dazzled by some evanescent phantom; and against those who make the whole a prophetic dream, insist that whether by day or by night it was a real sight. Say also whom it was for: not for Joshua's private encouragement only but to confirm the whole people, and to furnish posterity with proof of a kindness never duly considered. Then argue the identity by name and against opponents. Grotius and other moderns make this a created angel, following the Rabbis, who went further and fixed on Michael with nothing stronger than a verse in Daniel; but the apostle is a competent witness that it was Christ, and one who received worship cannot have been a creature. Be equally careful on the other side: Christ did not then become incarnate, and what appeared was a likeness of man, whether substantial body or outward form being needless to discuss. Answer the remaining difficulty -- how a captain who had never left can say he is now come -- from the common usage of Scripture, that God is said to come to us when his help is actually felt. And take the loosened shoe as a help to human weakness, since no place is holier than another except as God makes it so.

Begin by fixing the boundaries of the passage, since the chapter division here is among the most unfortunate in the Bible: this account runs on into the next chapter, whose first verse is a parenthesis, and readers who stop at the chapter's end are left unable to see what the appearance was for. Then argue the identity from three facts and let them stand: he accepted adoration, which a created angel dared not admit and which the angel in the Revelation expressly refused; the place was made holy by his presence, which is God's prerogative; and he is called Jehovah in the next chapter. Give Joshua his due as well -- an ordinary man seeing an armed figure with a drawn sword would have fled for the camp, and Joshua, probably slightly armed, walked up and questioned him. Close with the practical use. The manna had just failed, and a people much addicted to incredulity might have concluded that God had given them up; this vision assured them that the Angel of his presence went with the camp, and that their help came not by human might or power but from the Lord of hosts.

Compare this appearance with the one at Horeb and then contrast them. The identity of the two is proved by the same command on both occasions to loose the shoe from off the foot; but the bush burning and not consumed is the figure of suffering Israel in the furnace, in all whose affliction he was afflicted, while the man with the drawn sword is the sign of victory, God no longer suffering with and in his people but standing forth to lead them. Then read the answer strictly. He says neither for you nor for them, which means that Jehovah takes part in this conflict not as an ally and not as an adversary but as commander-in-chief. It is not Israel's quarrel in which they ask divine assistance; it is the Lord's own quarrel, and Israel and Joshua are but a division in his host, which is why these campaigns are always called the wars of the Lord. Press the point, because the conquest of Canaan is too often treated as an enterprise of the Israelites for which divine sanction was claimed afterwards.

debates.question: Who was the man with the drawn sword?

sides.position: The Son of God, since he accepted worship a created angel would have refused, the place was made holy by his presence, and he is called Jehovah in the next chapter

The same, argued against Grotius and the moderns who make him a created angel and against the Rabbis who name Michael on the strength of a verse in Daniel; but with the caution that Christ did not then become incarnate, what appeared being a likeness of man

The question of identity is left aside for the contrast with Horeb: the same command about the shoe proves the visions equal, but the bush unconsumed figures suffering Israel while the drawn sword is the sign of victory

debates.question: What does the refusal of both sides mean?

sides.position: That Jehovah takes part not as an ally and not as an adversary but as commander-in-chief; it is not Israel's quarrel in which divine help is sought but the Lord's own, Israel being a division in his host
That he came to preside over the chosen people, whom he honourably styles the Lord's host; the denial applies most properly to the second half of the question
That Joshua is captain only under him, and is about to be instructed in his conduct of the war

outliers.note: Alone turns the captain's refusal of both sides into a caution about how the conquest is described, insisting that these are the Lord's wars and not an Israelite enterprise for which divine sanction was claimed afterwards.

Alone attacks the chapter division, holding it among the most unfortunate in the Bible, since the account runs on into the next chapter and readers who stop at the chapter's end cannot see what the appearance was for.

themes: there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand
Art thou for us, or for our adversaries? And he said, Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come
Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy
